case_studies.title: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services
case_studies.abstract: Users of large language model (LLM) services receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred their charges. In broker-mediated agent workflows, calls arise after authorization and billing evidence spans service domains. A bill can count one genuine receipt twice and omit another. Valid metering evidence can also be attributed to the wrong execution. We present \textsc{TokenProv}, which uses authenticated provider acceptances to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges. An authenticated causal history links runtime attempts to the signed policy, and jointly signed handoffs bind intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. Handoffs submitted independently of the bill can reveal omitted calls. The auditor requires a one-to-one match between observable acceptances and settled receipts. For each acceptance, a common provider relation binds metered usage to the cache-dependent execution of the accepted input using the registered model and serving rules, and checks the charge under the pricing rule. To limit serving-path overhead, providers can use attested state transitions in trusted execution environments or defer proof generation until audit by committing to witnesses in receipts before settlement. The auditor recomputes the bill from the verified charges. We prove audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence. Across five models, \textsc{TokenProv} with signed provider receipts achieves 94.4--107.4\% of baseline throughput with 54--66\,ms of online non-LLM processing per request. In a separate eight-call replay, deferring scoped proofs reduces foreground protocol time from 1.20\,s to 8.65\,ms (99.28\%). The auditor rejects all 1,600 validly signed attack queries across 100 adaptive episodes.
case_studies.summary: TokenProv solves the problem of hidden or duplicated token charges in LLM services by using signed provider acceptances and causal histories to verify each billed call. The team built a verifier that matches observed acceptances with settlements, achieving near‑baseline throughput and low latency while detecting all attack attempts in tests. This is relevant for anyone managing LLM usage billing or ensuring fair cost allocation in multi‑provider cloud workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud LLM usage, step 1: collect signed provider receipts for every request. Step 2: run a TokenProv‑style verifier to match receipts with your billing system and flag any missing or duplicated calls. Step 3: integrate the verifier into your audit pipeline to enforce one‑to‑one billing and prevent over‑billing or fraud.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a practical issue—verifiable token billing—for LLM services that directly impacts IT engineers managing cloud SaaS billing. The solution is built, benchmarked, and demonstrates near‑line‑rate performance, indicating production readiness. It offers a clear, deployable workflow that can be integrated into existing billing systems or sold as a compliance service. The monetisation potential is substantial, though it requires specific billing platform integration, justifying a score of 20.

case_studies.title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
case_studies.abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.
case_studies.summary: The study reviews how large language models (LLMs) can be used to move whole software projects from one language or framework to another, showing that while module‑level changes work well, full repository migration still struggles with build reliability, behaviour testing, and non‑functional properties. They built a taxonomy of migration approaches, analysed 96 papers, and identified gaps in requirements support, agent coordination, and cost‑benefit assessment. This research is relevant: it highlights practical risks and offers a framework for planning LLM‑driven migrations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use the taxonomy to map your migration stages: 1) catalogue modules needing change, 2) choose an agent type (agentless, single or multi‑agent) that matches your build pipeline, 3) integrate environment feedback loops to catch runtime behaviour gaps before full deployment.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses LLM-assisted migration which is relevant to software engineering and deployment, giving moderate real-world impact. However, as a survey without a concrete implementation, the maturity is low, and monetisation potential is speculative but possible. The total score is 30, not below 30, so low_signal is false.

case_studies.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
case_studies.abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.
case_studies.summary: DELTA captures every design change made during exploration and stores the outcome, letting engineers analyse why some tweaks help while others hurt. It builds a memory of parent‑child interventions, predicts performance accurately and can surface root causes that improve IPC by up to 1.4%.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, this is not directly applicable to your day‑to‑day tasks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a niche simulation-based analysis tool for microarchitectural design, which is far removed from the day‑to‑day infrastructure concerns of UK IT engineers. While the method is demonstrably usable (released code, simulation results) and shows some predictive capability, it offers little immediate practical utility or commercial viability for the target audience. Thus the overall impact, maturity, and monetisation potential are all low, resulting in a total score below the 30 threshold.

case_studies.title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
case_studies.abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.
case_studies.summary: The paper presents a framework that lets large language model agents generate realistic, emotion‑conditioned responses to events, matching real social media patterns. It builds a hierarchical prompting system that feeds demographic, psychological, and context cues to the LLM and validates outputs against Facebook share data. The result shows the model can reproduce both polarized and consensus emotional trends, though it under‑expresses anger, indicating a need for further calibration.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, this is not directly applicable to your work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on emotional modeling in agent-based simulations, which is largely academic and not directly applicable to day‑to‑day IT infrastructure management or automation. While it uses LLMs, the work is a research prototype with no released code or production deployment, limiting its immediate utility for IT engineers. The monetisation potential is minimal because the methodology is too specialized for general SaaS or security tooling, and no clear commercial product or service emerges that could be offered within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.
case_studies.summary: The research shows how to trim an AI agent’s memory to keep only what matters, cutting input size by up to 71% while keeping performance. However, this is about LLM behaviour modelling, not cloud infra management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a technique for reducing state in LLM agents, but its direct applicability to existing IT infrastructure (Microsoft 365, AWS, etc.) is minimal. The approach appears to be in prototype stage with no released production-ready system, and there is no clear path for immediate monetisation or service offering within 90 days for IT engineers.
